Just now

Eighteen months ago, a Chinese startup nobody outside AI circles had heard of released a model called R1 and wiped out roughly a trillion dollars of US tech market value in a single week. That was DeepSeek’s opening move. Its second one, revealed this month, is quieter but arguably bigger: the company is designing its own AI chip, according to Reuters, so it no longer has to depend on Nvidia or Huawei to run the models that made it famous.
Three people familiar with the project told Reuters that DeepSeek has spent roughly a year quietly building out a chip-design team and working with semiconductor partners. This isn’t a training chip, the kind used to build a model in the first place.
It’s an inference chip, the hardware that does the work every time someone actually uses the thing. That distinction matters more than it sounds like it should.
Why inference, and why now
Training a frontier model is a one-time, brutally expensive project. You need the most powerful hardware money can buy, and you need it for months. Inference is different. It’s what happens every single time a user sends a query and gets an answer back, and as AI products scale into hundreds of millions of users, inference is where the real, recurring computing bill lives. It’s cheaper per chip, more forgiving on manufacturing precision, and it’s the fastest-growing slice of the entire AI hardware market. If you’re a company trying to escape a supplier, that’s the sensible place to start.
And DeepSeek has real reasons to want out. Its original R1 breakthrough ran on Nvidia’s H800, a China-specific chip Washington banned outright in late 2023. Since then, the company has leaned harder on Huawei, and orders for Huawei’s newest Ascend 950 reportedly surged across Chinese tech firms after that launch.
Nvidia’s share of China’s AI chip market has collapsed to something close to zero, not just from export bans but because Beijing has been actively steering domestic firms away from Nvidia hardware, even chips Washington had cleared for sale. Huawei has stepped into that vacuum and now controls roughly half of China’s $50 billion AI chip market.
So DeepSeek isn’t really choosing between Nvidia and Huawei anymore. It’s trying to avoid depending entirely on either one.
The full-stack bet
Here’s what makes this a genuinely interesting business story rather than just a geopolitics story: DeepSeek built its reputation on being lean. R1 became famous precisely because it delivered near-frontier performance at a fraction of the assumed cost, which is what spooked markets in the first place. A company like that doesn’t wander into chip design casually, silicon is capital-intensive, slow, and littered with the corpses of software companies that tried to become hardware companies and failed.
Two things make this bet look less reckless than it would have years ago:

• First, DeepSeek just closed its first outside funding round, reportedly around $7 billion, valuing the company between $52 billion and $59 billion, a notable reversal for a firm that had prided itself on self-funding. That’s real capital to burn on a multi-year hardware program with no guaranteed payoff.

• Second, if it succeeds, DeepSeek stops being “the Chinese startup with the cheap, clever models” and becomes something structurally different: a full-stack AI company that controls both the intelligence layer and the silicon underneath it. That’s a very small club, and membership tends to come with pricing power nobody else in the room has.
The part that isn’t guaranteed
None of this is close to done. Building a competitive AI chip from scratch is one of the hardest engineering problems in the industry, and DeepSeek is trying to do it while boxed in by the same export controls it’s trying to escape. Advanced foundries and high-bandwidth memory, the components that separate a good AI chip from a mediocre one, remain largely out of reach for Chinese firms cut off from the leading-edge manufacturing that Taiwan and a handful of other players still dominate. Inference chips are more forgiving on process node than training silicon, which is exactly why DeepSeek picked this lane to fight in. But “more forgiving” is not “easy.” Nvidia shares still dipped only modestly on the news (roughly 1.6%) which tells you the market sees this as a real threat over years, not a five-alarm fire today.
What this actually signals
Step back from the chip specs and the bigger picture is a global AI hardware map that’s splitting in two. For the past several years, the assumption was that everyone, everywhere, would run AI workloads on some flavor of Nvidia hardware, with export controls acting as a speed bump rather than a wall.
What’s happening in China now looks more like the construction of a genuinely parallel stack: domestic models, tuned for domestic chips, running on domestic manufacturing wherever possible, with companies like Huawei, Cambricon, and Hygon getting first-class support baked directly into DeepSeek’s newest models instead of being an afterthought.
For investors, that’s not an abstract geopolitical footnote. A world with two increasingly separate AI hardware ecosystems changes who has pricing power, which supply chains are actually resilient, and which companies’ moats are built on infrastructure that half the planet is now actively trying to route around. Nvidia’s dominance was never really in question in the West. It’s the assumption that this dominance was global and permanent that’s now the thing quietly cracking.
Two years ago, the consensus story was that no amount of national ambition could substitute for Nvidia’s manufacturing partners, its CUDA software ecosystem, or its decade-long head start. Export controls were supposed to be the enforcement mechanism that made that gap permanent. What’s actually happened is messier and more interesting: the controls slowed China down, but they also forced exactly the kind of urgency that produces breakthroughs nobody was pricing in.
R1 was one of those breakthroughs. A viable, homegrown inference chip would be another, and it would be the one that actually threatens Nvidia’s cash flow rather than just its reputation for having the smartest researchers in the room.
DeepSeek spent last year proving that a scrappy outsider could match the frontier on a fraction of the budget. This year, it’s testing whether that same instinct:
Do it cheaper and do it yourself.
It works just as well when the product isn’t software at all, but the silicon underneath it.
